opus-5.5.text:
That's really the central question for me. Why does deep learning work at all? Data like images or text live in enormous dimensions, so by naive counting you'd need astronomically many examples to learn anything. That's the curse of dimensionality. So the data must have structure, and the question is which structure, and how a network exploits it.

The structure we've focused on is hierarchical and compositional. An image is made of objects, objects of parts, parts of edges and textures. A sentence is made of clauses, clauses of phrases, phrases of words. Crucially, many low-level configurations mean the same thing at the next level. Different words or local patches can be synonyms: they play the same role in building the higher-level concept.

To study this, we built simple generative models, essentially random context-free grammars, which we call the Random Hierarchy Model. A class label generates a few high-level features, each of those generates lower-level features, and so on down to the input, with several equivalent production rules at each level. This lets you ask precise questions about how many examples a network needs.

What we find is that concepts emerge from statistics. Even though you can't see the hidden variables directly, the way low-level features correlate with each other, or with the label, depends only on which latent variable they encode. Two synonymous patches have the same correlations with their context. So once you have enough data to measure those correlations above sampling noise, you can group synonyms together, effectively discovering the latent variable, the concept. That gives a sample complexity that is polynomial in the dimension, not exponential, and you can predict how it scales with the vocabulary size and the number of synonyms.

And then the hierarchy builds on itself. Once the network has grouped the lowest-level synonyms, the next level becomes a lower-dimensional problem, and its correlations become detectable. So the representation is constructed layer by layer, and you can watch it happen. The network becomes insensitive to exchanging synonyms at a given level once it has seen enough data, and that invariance appears exactly when test performance improves. Deep networks can do this. Shallow ones, which can't build intermediate representations, can't.

There's a nice consequence for language models trained with next-token prediction. The amount of context you can exploit grows with the training set size, because correlations with more distant tokens are weaker and need more data to resolve. As data grows, the model resolves deeper levels of the hierarchy, which looks like the emergence of more abstract structure. That gives one possible explanation of power-law scaling curves, and of the sudden jumps you sometimes see, as successive levels of latent structure become statistically accessible.

So my view, in short: concepts are latent variables in a compositional generative process, they leave fingerprints in the correlations of the observable data, and depth is what lets a network turn those weak, local statistical signals into a hierarchy of invariant representations. Of course real data is messier than our models, but I think this captures something essential about why learning with relatively little data is possible.

r001.rationale: The response describes depth building hierarchical, invariant representations, but does not state that deep architectures have an implicit bias toward forming coarse-grained variables.

r002.rationale: It says concepts emerge from statistical correlations and connects that process to language models, where more training data makes deeper abstract structure accessible.

r003.rationale: It explains that synonymous features have the same correlations with their context and can therefore be grouped to discover the latent concept.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks, it's a pleasure to be here.

So the way I think about it comes from physics, and the central question for me has always been: why does learning work at all in high dimension? If you take a generic function on a space with a million dimensions, like an image, and you try to learn it from examples, the number of samples you need grows exponentially with the dimension. That's the curse of dimensionality. And yet deep networks learn images with maybe a million examples. So the data must have a very strong structure, and the architectures must be able to exploit it. The question of how concepts emerge is really the question of what that structure is and how the network latches onto it.

The hypothesis I find most compelling is that real data are hierarchical and compositional. A scene is made of objects, objects are made of parts, parts are made of simpler features, down to edges and textures. And the key point is that there is a lot of synonymy at each level. A face can have many kinds of eyes, a car can have many kinds of wheels, and the higher-level concept doesn't care which one you picked. So a "concept" at some level is really an equivalence class: a set of low-level configurations that are interchangeable with respect to what sits above them.

To make this precise, with my group we studied simple generative models of such data, essentially random hierarchy models, where a class generates a few high-level features, each high-level feature can be realized by several synonymous groups of lower-level features, and so on down to the input. The nice thing is you can compute how many samples a deep network needs to learn this. And what you find is that the sample complexity is polynomial in the dimension, not exponential. The exponential curse gets broken precisely because the network can learn the synonyms level by level.

Now, how does it do that from statistics? This is the part I like. At the lowest level, two patches are synonyms if they tend to co-occur with the same contexts, or more concretely, if they have the same correlations with the labels or with neighboring patches. So a network, during gradient descent, first becomes sensitive to these correlations. Once it has grouped synonyms together in the first layer, the representation becomes invariant to which synonym was used, and the problem at the next layer is effectively lower dimensional. Then the same mechanism repeats. Concepts emerge as the network discovers invariances, layer after layer, and each invariance is detected through correlations that only become statistically significant once you have enough data. That's why you see these plateaus or sudden drops in the loss as you increase the training set: a new level of the hierarchy becomes learnable.

What I find striking is that this also predicts the exponent in the scaling laws people observe empirically. If you ask how the error decays with the number of samples, in these models it's controlled by how many synonyms there are and how deep the hierarchy is, and you get power laws with exponents that are not universal but depend on the structure of the data. So in a sense the scaling laws are a fingerprint of the compositional structure.

And one more thing: this view says depth is not just about expressivity. A shallow network could in principle represent the same function, but it couldn't learn it with a polynomial number of samples, because it has no way to build the invariances incrementally. The architecture is doing the work of matching the hierarchy in the data. Convolutions give you locality, depth gives you composition, and gradient descent with enough data gives you the statistics to resolve the synonyms. When you put those three things together, concepts just fall out.

Of course these are toy models, and real data are messier. But I think the qualitative picture, that concepts are learned as invariances detected from correlations, one level at a time, is probably right, and it's testable. We're now trying to measure these things directly in trained networks.

r001.rationale: It describes gradient descent grouping synonymous features into invariant representations, making the next layer’s problem lower dimensional. This communicates coarse-graining across layers.

r002.rationale: It says concepts emerge from correlations and statistics in deep networks generally, but does not identify LLMs or diffusion models.

r003.rationale: It defines synonyms as configurations that co-occur with the same contexts, including correlations with neighboring patches, and says the network groups them.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is what we mean by a concept. In a statistical model, you might have some underlying variable that explains many observations. An object, for example, can appear under different lighting conditions or from different viewpoints. Recognizing it requires retaining what is shared across those observations while discarding some of the variation. In that sense, learning a concept and learning an invariance are closely related.

But saying that the information is present in the statistics does not yet explain how a network discovers it. You have to distinguish what can be inferred from the data, what can be represented by the architecture, and what is actually found by the learning dynamics. Those are different questions.

Depth gives you a way to compose representations. Features extracted at one layer can become the ingredients for features at the next. If the data have a hierarchical structure, that can be a very useful match. The difficult part is explaining when training exploits that structure, and how much data it needs to do so.

So I would approach this through simplified models where we know the underlying structure of the data. Then we can ask whether the network recovers that structure, whether its representation becomes insensitive to irrelevant transformations, and whether this explains its ability to generalize. That gives us something precise to study before we identify those representations with concepts in the richer, human sense.

r001.rationale: The response discusses compositional representations and invariance but does not state that deep architectures have an implicit bias toward forming coarse-grained variables.

r002.rationale: It says that information being present in the statistics does not explain how a network discovers it, so it does not claim concepts emerge from statistics alone.

r003.rationale: The response describes retaining shared information across observations, but does not explain concept formation as grouping configurations that predict similar surrounding contexts.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is what we mean by a concept. Operationally, you might say that a network has learned a concept when it can recognize something across variations that are irrelevant to the task. The pixels change, but the identity of the object remains the same. So the network has to discover which variations matter and which ones it can ignore.

Statistics can provide the information needed to do that, but the structure of the data is essential. Suppose observations are generated by a hierarchy of underlying variables: objects have parts, and those parts have more elementary features. A deep architecture can potentially exploit that hierarchy, reusing intermediate representations instead of learning every possible configuration separately. That can make a very large difference to how many examples you need.

But we should distinguish that possibility from an explanation of what a trained network actually does. A network can also exploit a correlation that works in the training distribution without learning the underlying structure we had in mind. Good prediction alone doesn't establish that it has acquired a concept in the stronger sense.

So, from a physics perspective, I would try to formulate simple models where we control the structure generating the data, and then ask: under what conditions does learning recover that structure? How does that depend on the number of examples, the architecture, and the learning dynamics? That gives us a way to turn the emergence of concepts into a concrete question, rather than assuming that depth automatically produces abstraction.

r001.rationale: It says deep architectures may exploit hierarchical data and reuse intermediate representations, but does not state an implicit bias toward forming coarse-grained variables.

r002.rationale: It says statistics can help, while emphasizing that data structure is essential; it does not claim concepts in LLMs or diffusion models emerge from statistics alone.

r003.rationale: It describes recognizing identities across irrelevant variations, but not grouping configurations that predict similar surrounding contexts.
